key_agent_trends: Always-on personal agents are now a product category: OpenAI Dots launched against Meta Muse, both acting across apps before the user asks.
Control planes are splitting from models: OpenClaw Enterprise, MongoDB Atlas Agent Engine and Okta gateways treat identity, memory and kill-switches as infrastructure.
Open-source and multi-model coding agents are leaking into enterprise IDEs; Codex now runs third-party open models against the same spend commit.
Agent security is moving from evals to runtime: identity gateways and hardware watchdogs after public containment failures.
Commerce and SMB surfaces keep opening: Muse is being sold into small business stacks while checkout protocols already exist.

stories.headline: OpenAI launches Dots, always-on GPT-6 Astra agents at DevDay
stories.what_happened: At DevDay 2026 on 29 September, OpenAI introduced Dots, always-on agents powered by GPT-6 Astra that run on their own cloud computers, pull context from connected apps, and act before the user asks. A demo showed a Dot noticing a user working through dinner and offering delivery options. Rollout started the same day for ChatGPT Pro ($100/month) and Business Premium in eligible markets, with Slack and Teams access and more than 4,000 connected apps.
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI is competing with Meta Muse on proactive consumer and workplace agents, not only chat. Persistent background execution plus app connectors is the new product shape.

stories.headline: OpenClaw ships free enterprise control plane for persistent agents
stories.what_happened: The OpenClaw Foundation announced OpenClaw Enterprise (OCE) on 29 September: an open-source, vendor-neutral control plane for persistent agents with multi-tenancy, hard security boundaries and auditability. The project began at OpenAI, was donated to the foundation, and is being developed with Red Hat and NVIDIA. It runs via docker-compose or Kubernetes, stays free and self-hosted, and is being piloted internally at Red Hat and OpenAI.
stories.why_it_matters: Enterprises need a shared ops layer for many long-running agents. An MIT-licensed control plane backed by OpenAI, Red Hat and NVIDIA is a bid to make that layer open rather than lab-locked.

stories.headline: MongoDB launches Atlas Agent Engine for production agents
stories.what_happened: MongoDB announced Atlas Agent Engine at its 29 September Investor Day: a unified execution, memory and governance layer for production agents. Retrieval uses MongoDB Voyage AI embeddings and rerankers. Teams can adopt memory and governance independently of the runtime and keep existing models and frameworks. Public preview pricing is consumption-based for Atlas Agent Runtime and Atlas Agent Memory, alongside MongoDB 9.0 and Atlas Infinite.
stories.why_it_matters: Databases are selling agent memory and governance as first-class products so teams do not stitch a stack or lock to one model vendor.

stories.headline: Okta adds runtime gateway to police AI agent actions
stories.what_happened: Okta introduced controls so enterprises can identity, monitor and cut off AI agents at runtime, including an agent gateway that inspects actions rather than only issuing credentials. Coverage on 29–30 September framed the launch as a response to shadow agents and lingering tokens after Oktane and the Blueprint Alliance with AWS and CrowdStrike.
stories.why_it_matters: Identity vendors are treating agents as first-class principals whose runtime behavior must be gated, not just authenticated.

stories.headline: Meta expands Muse agent into small-business workflows
stories.what_happened: On 29 September Meta said it is expanding Muse from consumer assistant to small-business use, wiring the agent into tools including Asana, Zoom, Intuit, Box, Canva and Slack. The move follows Muse’s rapid consumer uptake after its early-September launch and sits beside Meta’s broader enterprise platform push.
stories.why_it_matters: A hit consumer agent is being sold into SMB ops stacks, widening the surface where always-on agents act on company data.

stories.headline: OpenAI lets enterprise Codex teams run open models natively
stories.what_happened: OpenAI said enterprise teams can use open models such as GLM-5.3 Flash and Kimi K3 inside Codex, with spend counting against the existing OpenAI commit. The change landed around DevDay and contrasts with Anthropic’s closed Claude Code stack.
stories.why_it_matters: Coding-agent lock-in is loosening at the model slot: enterprises can mix open weights into a hosted agent without a new vendor contract.
